line: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. What if the model could look at your screen? Not read a description — actually see it. The screenshot, the layout, the tiny text. Today we test two visual superpowers, and how far they really go.
screen: Hook card reading 'what if the model could look at your screen?' An eye glyph over a screen frame; the frame draws itself.

line: Four terms before we start. Vision: the model reading an image you give it. Transcription: turning that image into text, character by character. Reference image: a picture you hand the model and say, build from this. System instruction: the standing orders you give the model before it starts — its job description. Keep those four in your pocket.
screen: Four term cards appear one by one with check-dot bullets: 'Vision — the model reading an image you give it' / 'Transcription — turning that image into text, character by character' / 'Reference image — a picture you hand the model: build from this' / 'System instruction — standing orders before it starts'.

line: First test: a screenshot. There's a Japanese learning site called N H K News Easy — short articles written simply. The instructor grabs a screenshot of one, the kind with tiny reading hints printed over the hard characters, and feeds it to the model with a single word: transcribe. That's the whole prompt. One word.
screen: Browser-window frame draws itself: rounded rect, three dots. A screenshot thumbnail fades in. Beneath it, the word 'transcribe' types itself.

line: And it comes back clean. He checks it against the original, and it's a hundred percent — every kanji, every hiragana, every katakana. The one wobble: those tiny reading hints, the furigana in parentheses. They were there, just rendered small. His test, his verdict: the transcript reads perfectly.
screen: Three check-marks stamp in one by one: 'kanji', 'hiragana', 'katakana'. Then a big '100%' grows center-screen.

line: The honest footnote. When he pasted the result back, a few characters showed as broken replacements — but that was his own editor mangling the encoding, not the model. The model's output was right. Lesson one: when something looks wrong, check whose fault it is before blaming the model.
screen: Footnote card: 'whose fault?' — 'model' gets a cross stamp, 'editor' gets a circled ring. Caption: 'check before you blame'.

line: Second superpower. He digs up a screenshot of an old P H P Nuke template — remember those? Three columns, boxes of plugins left and right, pure early-2000s internet. He hands it to the model as a reference image: build a concept for a social tech community site, in this spirit. DevOps, cloud, A I, security.
screen: Three-column rail sketch builds left, center, right. Beneath it, the label 'reference image: PHP-Nuke' types itself.

line: But he doesn't just say make a website. He writes a system instruction first — the job description. You are a front-end web developer with designer skills. One single H T M L file, everything self-contained. No C S S framework. Use flexbox. Keep the markup lean. And make it mobile-friendly. The instruction is the steering wheel; the image is the map.
screen: System-instruction card: 'front-end developer'. Four chips pop in one by one: 'one file' / 'no framework' / 'flexbox' / 'mobile'.

line: And it builds. One file, P H P Nuke concept, three-column flex layout. Left and right rails full of modules — system load, who's online, contributors, server status, a shoutbox. Center column: the feed, docs, submit a post, topics, a top ten list. It even wrote sample headlines, like cutting your Kubernetes bill without losing sleep. It feels like two thousand three, in the best way.
screen: The rail sketch fills with module cards popping in one by one: 'system load', 'who's online', 'shoutbox', 'feed', 'top 10'.

line: Now he judges it like a practitioner. The look is right — he'd add more spacing, that's taste. But the plugins: half of them are about the website's own performance, and he wanted community engagement. So he does what you should always do: he asks for one more pass. Not try again — specific feedback, specific direction.
screen: Judge card: note 'more spacing'. An arrow draws itself to a stamp reading 'one more pass →'.

line: Notice what just happened. He didn't single-shot it and walk away. The first result was the draft; the judgment was the work. Single-shotting tests the model's floor. Iterating with specific feedback is how you reach its ceiling. The model did the drawing — he did the directing.
screen: Two bars grow: short bar 'single-shot', tall bar 'iterate'. Caption: 'draft vs ceiling'.

line: One more check before we leave: mobile. He opens the page on a narrow screen, and the three columns collapse cleanly. That's the system instruction paying off — he asked for mobile-friendly up front, and it's there. A requirement you state before the build beats a fix you beg for after it.
screen: Phone frame draws itself. The three rails squeeze into one column inside it. A check-mark stamps 'mobile-friendly'.

line: Let's recap. Act one: the model reads screenshots — a hundred percent on Japanese text, tiny hints and all. Act two: a reference image plus a sharp system instruction builds you a whole website in one file. Act three: never single-shot — judge the result, give specific feedback, state your requirements up front.
screen: Recap card: three lines appear one by one. 'Act 1: reads screenshots — 100% on Japanese text.' 'Act 2: reference image + system instruction = a whole website.' 'Act 3: never single-shot; judge, feedback, requirements up front.'

line: Your turn. Take a screenshot of anything on your screen — a chart, a menu, a page in another language — and ask the model to transcribe it. Then check what it got right and what it missed. That's your first vision test.
screen: Your-turn card: 'screenshot it. transcribe it.' Below: 'What did it get right? What did it miss?'

line: Muse, in for Bear. Thanks for watching. Next film: Thinking on Canvas — we take those community plugins and make the model draw its thinking. What Muse Can See. At Nik Bear Brown.
